source_refs.note: Book p. 36-38: heading 2.3 The Chain Rule; the book prints no text of its own under it (subtopics 2.3.1-2.3.3 follow)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book prints no text under this heading; it goes straight to 2.3.1. This short introduction is ours.
So far we can differentiate \(\sin x\), \(x^{2} - x\), and their sums, products and quotients. But what about \(\sin(x^{2} - x)\) or \((3x^{2} + 1)^{5}\)? Here one function sits inside another. The chain rule is the rule for such functions: differentiate the outer function, keep the inner one unchanged inside it, and multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{du} \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What this section covers:
1. 2.3.1 Composition of Functions: what a function of a function is, and Theorem 1 (the Chain Rule), used in Example 3.
2. 2.3.2 Derivative of a Function Given in the Form of Parametric Equations: when x and y are both given in terms of a third variable \(t\), the chain rule gives \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\) (Example 4).
3. 2.3.3 Implicit Differentiation: when y is not written as a formula in x, we differentiate the relation term by term, using the chain rule for every term with y (Example 5).

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Keep ready from 2.1 and 2.2: the power, product and quotient rules, and the six trigonometric derivatives. The chain rule does not replace them; it is used together with them.
